absent: Locking rules, concurrency guarantees and calling contexts for audit, block, trace and zone interfaces.
Numeric values of ELF machine identifiers, page size, audit bitmask size and maximum field count.
Validation, permission checks and error codes for ioctls, netlink exchanges and rule installation.
Kernel side state machines for audit daemon lifecycle, key wrapping and zone transitions beyond the listed values.
Alignment, padding and endianness guarantees beyond stated member widths and orders.
Interpretation of reserved words, future feature bits and ignored name fields.

findings.text: Audit status selection uses eight distinct single bit flags in the low byte. The enabled indicator uses the lowest bit, the failure handling selector uses the next bit, followed in order by process identifier, rate limit, backlog limit, backlog wait timeout, lost count and actual wait time indicators, each occupying the next higher bit position.

Kernel audit capability advertisement uses seven low single bit flags for backlog limit, backlog wait time, executable path, extended exclusion, session identifier filtering, lost counter reset and filesystem filtering. The collective value is the combination of all seven, the latest version equals that combination, and two older version names equal the first and second single bits respectively.
Failure to record an audit event selects among three small integers. Silent loss uses zero, kernel message emission uses one, and immediate system halt uses two.

Audit architecture identifiers embed width, byte order and calling convention qualifiers in the high bits. The sixty four bit marker uses the top bit, the little endian marker uses the next bit, the convention field occupies two lower high bits with a mask covering both, and the MIPS64 N32 convention uses one specific pattern inside that field.

Early audit architecture values pair machine numbers with width and endian markers. Sixty four bit little endian forms are AUDIT_ARCH_AARCH64, AUDIT_ARCH_ALPHA and AUDIT_ARCH_IA64. Little endian thirty two bit forms are AUDIT_ARCH_ARCOMPACT, AUDIT_ARCH_ARCV2, AUDIT_ARCH_ARM, AUDIT_ARCH_C6X, AUDIT_ARCH_CRIS, AUDIT_ARCH_CSKY, AUDIT_ARCH_I386, AUDIT_ARCH_MIPSEL, AUDIT_ARCH_NDS32 and AUDIT_ARCH_NIOS2. Unqualified forms are AUDIT_ARCH_ARCOMPACTBE, AUDIT_ARCH_ARCV2BE, AUDIT_ARCH_ARMEB, AUDIT_ARCH_C6XBE, AUDIT_ARCH_FRV, AUDIT_ARCH_H8300, AUDIT_ARCH_HEXAGON, AUDIT_ARCH_M32R, AUDIT_ARCH_M68K, AUDIT_ARCH_MICROBLAZE, AUDIT_ARCH_MIPS, AUDIT_ARCH_NDS32BE, AUDIT_ARCH_OPENRISC, AUDIT_ARCH_PARISC and AUDIT_ARCH_PPC. Sixty four bit big endian forms are AUDIT_ARCH_MIPS64 and AUDIT_ARCH_PARISC64, with AUDIT_ARCH_MIPS64N32, AUDIT_ARCH_MIPSEL64 and AUDIT_ARCH_MIPSEL64N32 covering N32 convention and little endian sixty four bit combinations.

Later audit architecture values continue the same pairing. Unqualified forms are AUDIT_ARCH_S390, AUDIT_ARCH_SH, AUDIT_ARCH_SPARC and AUDIT_ARCH_XTENSA. Little endian thirty two bit forms are AUDIT_ARCH_RISCV32, AUDIT_ARCH_SHEL, AUDIT_ARCH_TILEGX32, AUDIT_ARCH_TILEPRO, AUDIT_ARCH_UNICORE and AUDIT_ARCH_LOONGARCH32. Sixty four bit big endian forms are AUDIT_ARCH_PPC64, AUDIT_ARCH_S390X, AUDIT_ARCH_SH64 and AUDIT_ARCH_SPARC64. Sixty four bit little endian forms are AUDIT_ARCH_PPC64LE, AUDIT_ARCH_RISCV64, AUDIT_ARCH_SHEL64, AUDIT_ARCH_TILEGX, AUDIT_ARCH_X86_64 and AUDIT_ARCH_LOONGARCH64.

Audit file watch permissions use four single bit flags with values one, two, four and eight for execute, write, read and attribute change respectively. The longest audit message text payload is eight thousand five hundred sixty bytes.

Audit netlink grouping defines an unused zero group, a best effort read only log group at one, and an internal upper bound marker. The public maximum equals the internal marker minus one, so only the read log group is usable.

Audit status exchange begins with selector mask, then enabled flag, failure action, daemon pid, rate limit, backlog limit, lost count and current backlog depth, then a union holding either legacy version or feature bitmap, and closes with configured wait timeout plus observed actual wait time. All members are thirty two bit unsigned values in the stated order.

Feature negotiation carries a format version followed by three thirty two bit words selecting which features are addressed, which are enabled, and which are locked. Teletype auditing status carries enabled and password logging flags as two thirty two bit words. The feature format version is one, feature indices zero and one denote login identifier handling, with one as the last valid index.

A feature index is accepted when it lies between zero and the last feature inclusive. Its mask is a single bit chosen by the low five bits of the index within a thirty two bit word. Unset user identifier and unset session identifier both use all bits set in an unsigned integer.

Audit rule exchange starts with flags, action and field count, followed by a syscall mask array sized by the bitmask constant, three parallel arrays sized by the maximum field constant holding field identifiers, values and per field modifiers, then a total string length and a trailing variable length byte area holding all string bodies.

Auxiliary vector tags zero through seventeen identify end of vector, ignored entry, program file descriptor, program header address, entry size, entry count, page size, interpreter base, flags, entry point, non ELF marker, real and effective user and group identifiers, optimization platform string, hardware capability hints and clock tick frequency, each tag using its position as its numeric value.

Higher auxiliary tags use scattered values. Secure mode uses twenty three, real platform string uses twenty four, sixteen random bytes address uses twenty five, extended capability hints use twenty six, restartable sequence feature size and alignment use twenty seven and twenty eight, further capability extensions use twenty nine and thirty, program filename uses thirty one, and minimal signal stack size uses fifty one.

Program invocation limits allow a single argument string up to thirty two pages and up to the largest signed thirty two bit count of strings. The interpreter probe buffer holds two hundred fifty six bytes. Auxiliary flag bit zero preserves the original argument zero and bit one marks a transparent interpreter, each exposed both as a bit position and as a single bit mask.

Three helpers build a contiguous set bit range between inclusive high and low positions. One targets native word width, one targets sixty four bit width, and one targets one hundred twenty eight bit width by combining single bit powers. Callers supply high then low positions.
User visible headers use unique include guard macros that expand to themselves to ensure single inclusion across translation units.

Block cryptography key management uses three fixed request layouts built from sixty four bit address and length pairs plus reserved words. Import carries raw key input pair and long term wrapped key output pair, generation carries only the long term output pair, and preparation carries long term input pair plus ephemeral output pair, each ending with four reserved words.

Block layer control entries share control group eighteen. Key import, generation and preparation are bidirectional exchanges numbered one hundred thirty seven through one hundred thirty nine. Discard and zone reset all for polling queues are simple commands numbered zero and one. Partition rescanning is a simple command numbered one hundred five.

Partition control passes an operation code, flags, payload length and user buffer address. Supported operations are add, delete and resize with values one through three. The partition descriptor holds sixty four bit start and length in bytes, a partition number, and two sixty four byte name areas for device and volume names that are currently ignored.

Block trace categories occupy distinct powers of two. Read through force unit access use the low sixteen bits, with a legacy end marker at the top of that range, while zone and write zeroes categories use sixty four bit positions sixteen through twenty two with a second end marker. Category values are promoted by shifting left sixteen positions to form the high half of combined actions.

Trace action identifiers form an ordered sequence from queue through driver data, with queue, merges, allocation, sleep, requeue, issue, completion, plug handling, insertion, split, bounce placeholder, remap, abort, driver data and zone plug handling, plus a separate high flag marking cgroup origin. Notification identifiers use zero through two for process mapping, timestamp and text message, reusing the same high cgroup flag.

Combined codes pair each low action with its shifted category. Queue family actions pair with the queue category, requeue with requeue, issue and completion with their matching categories, driver data with driver data, zone append completion with zone append, zone plug handling with queue, and process, timestamp and message notifications with the notify category, while split and bounce stay unshifted. The stream magic is 0x65617400 and the two format versions are seven and eight.

First generation trace records hold magic with version, sequence, nanosecond time, sector, byte length, combined action, process identifier, device, processor, completion error and trailing data length. Second generation widens the action to sixty four bits, reorders process identifier before action, and adds twelve pad bytes. Remap records hold source and destination devices plus source sector in mixed endian widths.
Tracing setup progresses through three ordered states for configured, active and halted capture. Device path buffers for the two setup generations hold thirty two and sixty four bytes respectively.

User setup for first generation carries device name output, sixteen bit action mask, buffer size and count, logical block range, and process filter. Second generation widens the name, uses a sixty four bit action mask, adds a flag word and eleven reserved sixty four bit words while keeping size, count, range and process fields.

Zoned block types use one through three for conventional, sequential write required and sequential write preferred. Zone conditions use zero through four for no write pointer, empty, implicitly opened, explicitly opened and closed, plus thirteen through fifteen for read only, full and offline, with an alias value of all low bits set selecting active zones. Reporting uses bit zero to request capacity output and the top bit to allow cached data.

Zone descriptors hold sixty four bit start, length, write pointer and capacity, single byte type, condition, nonsequential resource and reset recommendation indicators, plus reserved areas. Report headers hold start sector, zone count and flags followed by a variable length array of descriptors. Range descriptors hold start sector and sector count as two sixty four bit values.

Several exchanges carry trailing variable data or user addresses that require length validation. Audit rules append string bytes sized by an explicit length, zone reports append a descriptor array sized by a count, trace records append bytes sized by a length field, partition control dereferences a user buffer with separate length, and cryptography and second generation trace setup carry reserved words that must be zeroed for forward compatibility.

These headers export user kernel contracts for audit control, auxiliary vectors, program loading limits, block cryptography, partitioning, block tracing and zoned storage, centered on status, rule, key, partition, trace and zone structures plus their numeric tags and control numbers.
